📋 What is a CI Brief?

A Competitive Intelligence Brief is a deal-specific document that arms sales teams with everything they need to win against a specific competitor. Unlike generic battlecards, CI Briefs are tailored to:

  • The specific deal context (industry, size, stage)
  • Known competitor activity in the account
  • Intelligence gathered from discovery calls
  • Historical win/loss data for similar situations

The best CI Briefs are actionable—they give sales reps specific questions to ask, responses to prepare, and proof points to reference.

📊 Example CI Brief
SALES-READY BRIEF

Acme Manufacturing — S/4HANA Cloud vs. Oracle Fusion

📅 Generated: Nov 12, 2026 👤 Prepared for: Sarah Chen, Enterprise AE ⏱️ Stage: Technical Evaluation

📍 Deal Context

Account
Acme Manufacturing Corp.
Industry
Discrete Manufacturing
Revenue
$1.8B annually
Employees
6,500 global
Deal Size
$2.4M TCV
Decision Date
Q1 2027

📝 Executive Summary

Acme is a greenfield opportunity—they're running JD Edwards EnterpriseOne and evaluating both SAP S/4HANA Cloud and Oracle Fusion Cloud ERP. Oracle has a relationship with the CFO from his previous company. Our champion is the VP of Operations who saw S/4HANA at a peer company (Precision Parts Inc.) and was impressed with the manufacturing depth.

Key insight: The CIO is concerned about Oracle's manufacturing module maturity. They attempted an Oracle implementation at his last company (canceled after 14 months). We need to amplify this concern while demonstrating S/4HANA's manufacturing pedigree.

Competitive status: Oracle submitted proposal two weeks ago. They're leading with "single cloud platform" messaging and aggressive first-year pricing. We're scheduled for technical deep-dive next Tuesday.

🔍 Competitor Intelligence

💰 Oracle's Pricing Strategy

Oracle is offering a 40% first-year discount with aggressive SaaS conversion incentives. However, years 2-5 normalize at list price with 3-5% annual escalators.

  • First-year discount: ~$400K savings vs. SAP
  • 5-year TCO: Likely $200-300K MORE than SAP after escalators
  • Hidden costs: Data conversion, custom reports, integration middleware
Source: Win/Loss DB, Similar Deal (Q3 2026)

🏭 Oracle Manufacturing Gaps

Oracle Fusion's manufacturing module is less mature than their financial suite. Common issues we've heard from evaluators:

  • Shop floor integration requires middleware (no native MES connectivity)
  • Production planning lacks demand-driven MRP capabilities
  • Quality management is bolt-on, not embedded
  • Limited discrete manufacturing reference customers in their size range
Source: Analyst call (Gartner), Q2 2026

👤 Oracle's Internal Champion

CFO Michael Torres worked with Oracle at his previous company (Midwest Industrial). That implementation was primarily financials-focused. He may not fully understand manufacturing requirements.

  • Relationship is real but not manufacturing-specific
  • Opportunity: Get VP Ops to educate CFO on manufacturing complexity
  • Risk: CFO may fast-track decision based on relationship trust
Source: LinkedIn, Discovery call notes

🪤 Trap Questions for Oracle

Arm your champion to ask these questions when Oracle presents. Each exposes a known weakness:

"Can you show us a discrete manufacturing customer at our scale who's live on Fusion ERP with shop floor integration?"
Setup: Oracle's manufacturing references are primarily process industries (chemicals, food). Discrete manufacturing at $1B+ scale is thin.
Follow-up: "And can we speak with their VP of Operations directly about their shop floor experience?"
"Walk us through how production planning handles sudden demand spikes—do you support demand-driven MRP?"
Setup: Oracle's planning module is traditional MRP. SAP's DDMRP is a differentiator for companies with volatile demand.
Follow-up: "How did your manufacturing customers handle COVID demand volatility specifically?"
"What's the integration architecture for connecting to our Rockwell PLCs and Siemens MES?"
Setup: Oracle requires third-party middleware for shop floor integration. SAP has native manufacturing integration hub.
Follow-up: "Who provides support when there's an integration issue during production?"
"Show us the 5-year TCO including annual price escalators and any usage-based components."
Setup: Oracle's Year 1 discount obscures higher long-term costs. Always normalize to 5-year view.
Follow-up: "And what happens to pricing if we exceed the named user count in Year 3?"

🛡️ Objection Handlers

❌ "Oracle is offering a 40% discount in Year 1—SAP can't match that."
"You're right, we won't win a Year 1 price war. But let's look at what you're actually buying. Model the 5-year TCO including Oracle's 3-5% annual escalators, the middleware for shop floor integration, and the custom development for manufacturing reports. We've seen deals where Oracle's 5-year cost exceeds SAP by 15-20%. Let's build that model together for your specific scope."
📊 Reference: Precision Parts Inc. TCO analysis showed Oracle 18% higher over 5 years.
❌ "Our CFO has worked with Oracle before—he's comfortable with them."
"That's valuable experience. What did Michael implement at Midwest Industrial? My understanding is it was primarily financials. Manufacturing ERP is a different animal—shop floor integration, quality loops, production scheduling. I'd love to connect your VP of Operations with a peer who evaluated both for a manufacturing-heavy implementation. Different requirements, different decision criteria."
📞 Reference: Can arrange call with VP Ops at Precision Parts (similar journey).
❌ "Oracle has a single cloud platform—SAP's architecture seems more complex."
"Single platform sounds simpler on paper. But ask Oracle about manufacturing specifically: Where does the production scheduling engine run? How does quality data flow to the shop floor? You'll find they're assembling multiple acquisitions behind that 'single' interface. SAP S/4HANA was built ground-up for manufacturing—40 years of production logic in one codebase, not stitched together from M&A."
📋 Reference: Gartner MQ positions SAP as Leader in Manufacturing ERP specifically.

🎯 Recommended Talk Track

Opening

"Before we dive into demos, I want to acknowledge something: you're going to see polished presentations from both SAP and Oracle. What I'd encourage you to do is ask us both the hard manufacturing questions—shop floor integration, quality loops, production planning for volatile demand. That's where the differences become clear."

Differentiation

"Oracle does financials well—no argument there. But manufacturing is where SAP started. We have 40 years of production logic built into S/4HANA. Oracle's manufacturing module came from acquisitions—JD Edwards, Agile PLM, different architectures stitched together. When you're running a $1.8B manufacturing operation, that architectural difference matters."

Call to Action

"Here's what I'd suggest: Let's schedule a manufacturing-specific deep dive with your VP of Operations and plant managers. Not a generic demo—a working session on your actual production scenarios. And let's connect you with Precision Parts—similar size, similar journey, made the SAP decision 18 months ago. Hear it from a peer."

✅ Pre-Meeting Actions

  • Schedule reference call: Precision Parts VP Ops → Acme VP Ops
  • Build 5-year TCO comparison model with realistic Oracle escalators
  • Prepare manufacturing deep-dive demo: MES integration + quality + planning
  • Brief our champion (VP Ops) on trap questions before Oracle's next meeting
  • Get Gartner MQ manufacturing positioning slide for CIO presentation
  • Research CFO's Oracle history at Midwest Industrial (scope, outcomes)
